title: Living or Not? Viruses and Bacteria

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: All the chemical reactions that take in and use energy in a living thing are called {{c1::metabolism}}.
cards.quote: take in and use energy (all the chemical reactions that do this are called metabolism)

cards.front: A virus is an infectious agent made of {{c1::genetic material}} inside a protein coat.
cards.quote: A virus is an infectious agent made of genetic material inside a protein coat.

cards.front: Why are viruses classed as nonliving while bacteria are living?
cards.back: A bacterium is a cell with its own ribosomes and metabolism. A virus is not a cell, has no metabolism of its own, and new copies are built only inside a host cell.
cards.quote: A bacterium is a cell with its own ribosomes and metabolism.

cards.front: On a living-or-not checklist, you compare a virus outside a cell with a virus inside a host cell. Which box changes, and does the virus become alive?
cards.back: The reproduce box changes to "only with a host cell." The cell and metabolism boxes stay unmet, so the virus is still classed nonliving.
cards.quote: The cell and metabolism boxes stay unmet, so the classification does not change.

cards.front: Some giant viruses carry more than a thousand genes. Why does that not make them living, and what does it show about what separates viruses from bacteria?
cards.back: Under a definition based on cells and metabolism, they are still nonliving. Genes cannot be what separates a virus from a bacterium, because a virus can carry many.
cards.why: Rests on the cell-and-metabolism definition used in this course.
cards.quote: If a virus can carry that many genes, genes cannot be what separates it from a bacterium.

cards.front: Some living bacteria also depend on host cells. Why does needing a host not settle whether something is alive?
cards.back: Those bacteria are still cells with their own ribosomes and metabolism. Needing a host does not decide the case by itself; the cell and metabolism evidence matters.
cards.quote: Scientists still discuss definitions of life, and some living bacteria also depend on host cells, so needing a host does not decide the case by itself.

cards.front: What is a prokaryote?
cards.back: A one-celled living thing with no nucleus and, typically, no membrane-covered organelles. Bacteria are prokaryotes.
cards.quote: Bacteria are prokaryotes: one-celled living things with no nucleus and, typically, no membrane-covered organelles.

cards.front: Your cells are {{c1::eukaryotes}}, which usually have a nucleus.
cards.back: Mature red blood cells lose theirs.
cards.quote: Your cells are eukaryotes, which usually have a nucleus; mature red blood cells lose theirs.

cards.front: Where is the DNA of a typical bacterium, and what is special about that region?
cards.back: In the nucleoid, a region with no membrane around it.
cards.quote: DNA in the nucleoid, a region with no membrane around it

cards.front: What does a bacterial cell wall do?
cards.back: It helps keep the cell from bursting when water rushes in. Many bacteria have one; viruses do not.
cards.quote: Helps keep the cell from bursting when water rushes in

cards.front: What is a bacterial flagellum, and how does it work?
cards.back: A corkscrew-shaped tail that spins to push the cell through water.
cards.quote: A corkscrew-shaped tail that spins to push the cell through water

cards.front: What is a viral envelope, and what does it do?
cards.back: A fatty layer outside the capsid on some viruses. It helps some viruses enter cells.
cards.quote: Envelope helps some viruses enter cells

cards.front: A virus has no ribosomes. How does it get its proteins made?
cards.back: It uses the host cell's ribosomes. Ribosomes build proteins; a bacterium has its own, a virus does not.
cards.quote: A bacterium is a cell with its own ribosomes and metabolism.

cards.front: A virus that infects only bacteria is exposed to a mixture of bacterial, plant and animal cells. Which cells can it enter, and why?
cards.back: Only cells with receptors its surface proteins fit, such as its bacterial hosts. Each virus enters only certain cells.
cards.quote: Each virus can enter only certain cells, because proteins on its surface must fit receptors on the host cell.

cards.front: A virus that infects bacteria is called a {{c1::phage}}.
cards.quote: A virus that infects bacteria is called a phage.

cards.front: Which energy and carbon sources define a heterotroph, a photoautotroph and a chemoautotroph?
cards.back: Heterotroph: energy and carbon from carbon compounds it takes in. Photoautotroph: energy from light, carbon from carbon dioxide. Chemoautotroph: energy from chemicals, carbon from carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: Every living cell needs energy to do work and carbon to build its parts.

cards.front: A bacterium lives in a dark deep-sea vent, takes in carbon dioxide and gets energy from iron compounds. Which group is it?
cards.back: A chemoautotroph: its energy comes from chemicals and its carbon from carbon dioxide. There is no light, so it is not a photoautotroph.
cards.quote: Every living cell needs energy to do work and carbon to build its parts.

cards.front: Some bacteria use light for energy but take carbon from other living things. Which row of the energy table fits them?
cards.back: Neither row fits cleanly. Energy matches a photoautotroph and carbon matches a heterotroph. Energy and carbon sources are separate questions.
cards.quote: Energy source and carbon source are separate questions, so the three groups are a useful simplification.

cards.front: Rickettsia grow only inside other cells. Are they living, and why?
cards.back: Yes. They are still living cells with their own ribosomes and metabolism, though they take some energy molecules and nutrients from the host.
cards.quote: They are still living cells with their own ribosomes and metabolism, though they take some energy molecules and nutrients from the host.

cards.front: Most viruses are about {{c1::20 to 300 nm}} across.
cards.back: Typical bacteria are about 1 to 5 μm long, so they are larger.
cards.quote: Most viruses are about 20 to 300 nm across.

cards.front: An influenza particle is about 100 nm across and an E. coli cell is about 2 μm long. About how many particles lined up match the cell's length?
cards.back: Convert 2 μm to 2,000 nm. Then 2,000 nm ÷ 100 nm = about 20 particles.
cards.quote: A micrometer (μm) is a thousandth of a millimeter, and a nanometer (nm) is a thousandth of a micrometer.

cards.front: How many of the largest round influenza particles (120 nm) fit along a 2 μm E. coli cell?
cards.back: 2 μm = 2,000 nm. 2,000 ÷ 120 is about 17 particles.
cards.quote: A micrometer (μm) is a thousandth of a millimeter, and a nanometer (nm) is a thousandth of a micrometer.

cards.front: Why must a scientist report how a sample was prepared when giving a virus size? Use the T4 phage head as an example.
cards.back: Preparation changes the measurement. The T4 head measured about 100 × 85 nm in liquid and 75 × 60 nm after drying.
cards.quote: The T4 head measured about 100 × 85 nm in liquid and 75 × 60 nm after drying.

cards.front: Pond mud grows dark mineral specks. You compare fresh mud jars with jars of the same mud heated to kill microbes. Why use at least three jars per group?
cards.back: Repeated trials mean one odd jar does not decide the result.
cards.quote: Repeated trials: at least three jars in each group, so one odd jar does not decide the result.

cards.front: In the pond mud test, specks also form in the heated jars. What does that suggest, and what does it not prove even if specks form only in fresh jars?
cards.back: Specks in heated jars point to a chemical reaction that needs no life. Even if only fresh jars show them, that does not prove the bacteria use that chemical for energy.
cards.quote: Specks in the heated jars too would point to a chemical reaction that needs no life.

cards.front: Why can only living host cells, such as cells lining your nose, produce new copies of a virus?
cards.back: The virus is not a cell and has no metabolism of its own, so it needs a living cell to build copies.
cards.quote: Only living host cells, such as the cells lining your nose, can build new copies of it.
